newsitem.title: UK: Rejected U.S. prison shop arrives in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Rejected U.S. prison shop arrives in Britain.

text.p: A five-deck U.S.-built prison barge arrived in Britain on Thursday to help ease an acute jail shortage, prompting fears of a "floating Alcatraz" being moored off the nation's scenic southern coast.
The 18-year-old grey steel vessel edged at noon into Portland harbour, a tourist haven in the English county of Dorset, drawing an immediate protest from residents and penal reform activists.
One called the Resolution -- now to be known as Her Majesty's Prison (HMP) Weare -- a "nightmare" for inmates. Another described it as an eyesore on the stunning English sea front.
"We don't want to be known as the Alcatraz of Britain," said one local councillor in reference to the infamous U.S. island prison in San Francisco Bay.

The ship's last owner was New York's Department of Correction, which used the ship as a drug rehabilitation centre. It abandoned the barge as too costly and left it to rust in the Hudson River for five years.
A New York senator was "delighted" to be rid of it. "Buying that barge was a stupid decision that cost this city a lot of money," Britain's Guardian newspaper quoted the senator as saying.
New York had planned to sell the ship for scrap but in January the British government offered four million pounds ($6.4 million).
"If permission is given it would be about a month before we get prisoners aboard," a British prison service spokeswoman said.
The 480 inmates would be "C" category -- on a scale from "A" to "D" -- and could have committed crimes from fraud to murder.
Before any inmates settle in, the government must find a home for the ship, though it needs no persmission to berth it.
Councillors on the Isle of Portland -- which already houses two penal institutions -- aim to block the ship, saying it would scupper their schemes for a marina to attract pleasure craft.
The English Tourist Board has also criticised the plans to moor the towering ship at a "stunning geographic location".
The environment minister is due to rule on the matter next week. If permission is denied, "we'd think again. We have plans for other sites in the country," the prisons spokeswoman.

The number of prisoners in England and Wales has risen about 6,000 in the past year to around its capacity of 60,000 as the Conservative government gets tough on law and order ahead of a general election due within weeks.
Prison ships have not seen regular use in Britain since Victorian days, prompting concern that a harsh new penal era is dawning.
The government is already trying to meet the cell shortfall by converting old holiday and army camps into jails and hopes to copy some of the toughest U.S. punitive programmes.

"We are always taking the ideas America has rejected, like the boot camps and prison ships, rather than their best practices. It's very important to have access to the outside world and a ship is not appropriate," said Frances Crook, director of the independent Howard League for Penal Reform.

Yet the ship is no sin bin. Formerly a British troop carrier in the Falklands War, the Weare has been refitted with a chapel, library, squash courts and swimming pools. The sprawling recreation area is on the top deck and any prisoner seeking to escape would face a sheer drop of some 90 feet (25 metres).
